He wants a SECONDARY income-stream business he can largely build himself (pure software / AI preferred; hardware tolerated via mech-eng friends but penalized). Mark every major feasibility claim VERIFIED / ASSUMED / UNVERIFIED. Cite source URLs inline. Be specific and quantified. Use the Write tool to create the file (create the folder path as needed).

STEP 4 — Return the structured scorecard via the required schema. Score honestly and skeptically — if web research reveals entrenched competitors or fatal feasibility gaps, say NO-GO. The "founder_fit" score must reflect that pure-software ideas suit Hooman best and hardware adds risk.

4	**Domains explored**: Wire insulation AI inspection, cable partial discharge monitoring, paper formation sensing, paper web-break prediction, paper coating weight optimization, ceramic kiln thermal optimization, ceramic glaze defect vision, ceramic dimensional control, wire tensile testing automation, paper moisture profiling

8	## Step 1: Technology Discovery
9	
10	### 1. AI-Enhanced Wire Insulation Surface Inspection
11	- **Domain**: Wire & cable manufacturing
12	- **Breakthrough**: Edge-deployable vision transformers (ViT) running on $200 inference cards (Hailo-8, Jetson Orin NX) now achieve >99% defect classification at line speeds >600m/min, enabling replacement of $80-150K SIKORA/Pixargus surface inspection systems with $15-25K camera+edge-AI rigs.
13	- **TRL**: 7
14	- **Time to product**: 6-9 months
15	- **Status**: PROMOTED
16	- **Reasoning**: Wire and cable surface inspection is dominated by expensive legacy systems (SIKORA, LaserLinc FlawSense, Clinton spark testers). Mid-market cable manufacturers (500+ globally doing $5-50M revenue) cannot justify $100K+ systems. An AI-first approach on commodity cameras can undercut by 80%.
17	
18	### 2. Partial Discharge Pattern Recognition for MV Cable QC
19	- **Domain**: Wire & cable manufacturing (medium voltage)
20	- **Breakthrough**: ML models trained on partial discharge (PD) acoustic signatures can now classify insulation defect types (voids, contaminants, delamination) in real-time during cable production, rather than post-production testing.
21	- **TRL**: 5-6
22	- **Time to product**: 12-18 months
23	- **Status**: REJECTED
24	- **Reasoning**: TRL too low for the timeline. MV cable is also a smaller niche with long qualification cycles. Existing PD testing companies (HVPD, Prysmian in-house) serve the market. Regulatory certification requirements for MV cable testing add barriers.
25	
26	### 3. Paper Formation Analysis via Transmitted-Light AI Vision
27	- **Domain**: Paper & pulp industry
28	- **Breakthrough**: High-speed line-scan cameras with transmitted-light backlight + CNN analysis can now map fiber distribution uniformity (formation) in real-time at paper machine speeds (1500m/min), replacing expensive beta-ray or radioactive formation sensors.
29	- **TRL**: 7
30	- **Time to product**: 9-12 months
31	- **Status**: PROMOTED
32	- **Reasoning**: Traditional paper formation measurement relies on $200-500K QCS systems from Valmet, ABB, or Honeywell. Smaller paper mills (there are 5000+ globally under $100M revenue) either cannot afford full QCS or use offline lab testing. A $30-50K inline formation sensor using vision AI could serve this massive underserved segment.
33	
34	### 4. Paper Web-Break Prediction from Process Data
35	- **Domain**: Paper & pulp industry
36	- **Breakthrough**: Time-series transformer models can now predict web breaks 5-15 minutes in advance using existing sensor data (stock flow, consistency, tension, moisture), reducing broke by 20-40%. Each web break costs $5-50K in lost production.
37	- **TRL**: 6-7
38	- **Time to product**: 6-9 months
39	- **Status**: PROMOTED
40	- **Reasoning**: Web breaks are the #1 source of unplanned downtime in paper manufacturing. Valmet and ANDRITZ have announced "autonomous operations" strategies but their solutions are bundled into $1M+ DCS upgrades. A standalone SaaS that connects to existing process historians (OPC-UA) and predicts breaks could serve mills without full automation upgrades.
41	
42	### 5. Paper Coating Weight Optimization via NIR + ML
43	- **Domain**: Paper & pulp industry
44	- **Breakthrough**: Low-cost NIR spectrometers ($5-15K) combined with ML models can now measure coating weight, smoothness, and uniformity inline, approaching the accuracy of expensive scanning-frame QCS systems.
45	- **TRL**: 6
46	- **Time to product**: 12-15 months
47	- **Status**: REJECTED
48	- **Reasoning**: While the technology is promising, the competitive density is high. Valmet IQ, NDC/Nordson, and ABB all offer coating weight measurement as part of their QCS. Eigen Innovations already offers thermal AI for paper and packaging. The differentiation would be insufficient.
49	
50	### 6. Ceramic Kiln Energy Optimization via Thermal AI
51	- **Domain**: Ceramics & tile production
52	- **Breakthrough**: LWIR thermal cameras + ML can map temperature distribution across roller kilns in real-time, optimizing firing curves to reduce natural gas consumption by 8-15% while maintaining quality. Gas is 30-40% of tile production cost.
53	- **TRL**: 7
54	- **Time to product**: 6-9 months
55	- **Status**: PROMOTED
56	- **Reasoning**: The ceramic tile industry ($196B market) uses roller kilns consuming massive energy. Most mid-size tile plants (1000+ globally) rely on manual thermocouple readings and fixed firing profiles. No dominant AI-specific kiln optimization startup exists - SACMI sells kiln hardware but not AI optimization layers.
57	
58	### 7. Ceramic Glaze Defect Detection via Hyperspectral Vision
59	- **Domain**: Ceramics & tile production
60	- **Breakthrough**: SWIR/VNIR hyperspectral line-scan cameras can detect glaze composition anomalies (crazing precursors, thickness variation, contamination) before firing, when correction is still possible, rather than post-fire inspection.
61	- **TRL**: 6
62	- **Time to product**: 12-15 months
63	- **Status**: REJECTED
64	- **Reasoning**: SACMI already offers FlawMaster and ProcessMaster vision systems specifically for ceramic tile inspection. Durst has Gamma Vision. The competitive density is 4+ (SACMI/Italvision, System Ceramics, Durst, various Chinese players). Pre-fire detection angle is interesting but hyperspectral hardware adds cost and complexity.
65	
66	### 8. Wire Tensile Testing Automation via Acoustic Emission
67	- **Domain**: Wire & cable manufacturing
68	- **Breakthrough**: Acoustic emission sensors + ML can predict wire tensile strength and elongation non-destructively inline, replacing periodic destructive pull testing that wastes material and creates testing bottlenecks.
69	- **TRL**: 5
70	- **Time to product**: 15-18 months
71	- **Status**: REJECTED
72	- **Reasoning**: TRL too low. Acoustic emission for tensile prediction is still largely academic. Wire manufacturers have well-established destructive testing protocols. The ROI calculation is weak - destructive testing waste is a small fraction of production cost.
73	
74	### 9. Ceramic Tile Dimensional Control via Structured Light
75	- **Domain**: Ceramics & tile production
76	- **Breakthrough**: Commodity structured-light 3D scanners (Orbbec, etc.) + edge AI can measure tile flatness (warpage, curvature, edge straightness) at conveyor speed post-kiln, replacing $150-250K contact measurement systems.
77	- **TRL**: 7
78	- **Time to product**: 6-9 months
79	- **Status**: PROMOTED
80	- **Reasoning**: Tile dimensional control is critical (warpage = the #1 reject reason post-firing). Current systems are expensive (LMI Gocator, Keyence) or manual (calibrated rulers/gauges). Mid-size tile plants in India, Brazil, Turkey, and SE Asia often lack any automated dimensional QC.
81	
82	### 10. Paper Moisture Profile Optimization via Microwave Sensing + ML
83	- **Domain**: Paper & pulp industry
84	- **Breakthrough**: Non-contact microwave moisture sensors (cavity perturbation technique) combined with ML can map cross-direction moisture profiles at much lower cost than scanning-frame infrared systems, enabling closed-loop dryer control.
85	- **TRL**: 6
86	- **Time to product**: 12-15 months
87	- **Status**: REJECTED
88	- **Reasoning**: Moisture measurement is the most competitive QCS segment. Every major player (Valmet, ABB/Accuray, Honeywell, NDC/Nordson) offers moisture sensors. Microwave approaches exist (TEWS, Berthold). Competitive density is 5+.

95	- **Competitors found**: SIKORA (X-RAY 6000, CENTERVIEW), LaserLinc (FlawSense), Pixargus (ProfilControl), Zumbach (ODAC series), Clinton Instrument (spark testers). These are all legacy systems costing $80-200K.

97	- **Differentiation angle**: Software-first approach using commodity cameras ($2-5K) + edge AI inference ($500-2000) vs. proprietary hardware. SaaS model with per-meter pricing vs. $100K+ capex. 80% of defect detection capability at 15% of the cost.
98	- **Status**: PROMOTED
99	- **Reasoning**: Incumbents are hardware-centric German/Swiss companies selling $100K+ systems. No startup is offering AI-first wire surface inspection at the mid-market price point. The gap between "spark tester only" ($5-15K, finds pinholes but not surface defects) and "full surface inspection" ($100K+) creates a clear wedge.

101	### Paper Formation Analysis via Transmitted-Light AI Vision
102	- **Competitors found**: Valmet IQ (full QCS including formation), Procemex (web inspection, 1100+ systems), ABB/Accuray (QCS). However, these are bundled into $500K-2M QCS packages.

104	- **Differentiation angle**: Standalone formation-only sensor at 1/10th cost, retrofit to any machine without DCS integration.

While standalone low-cost formation sensing is underserved, the big players could easily offer a stripped-down product. Paper mills also prefer integrated QCS solutions. Market entry would require competing against very established players with deep paper industry relationships.

A vendor-agnostic SaaS that reads from OPC-UA historians and predicts breaks has no direct competitor. The 5000+ small/mid paper mills worldwide (each losing $500K-2M/year to breaks) represent a massive underserved market.

116	- **Competitors found**: SACMI (kiln hardware/controls), System Ceramics (kiln systems), Nabertherm (smaller kilns). These sell kiln hardware, not AI optimization software. Eigen Innovations serves paper/plastics thermal AI but NOT ceramics kilns.

118	- **Differentiation angle**: Retrofit thermal cameras + ML on existing kilns. No hardware replacement needed. ROI is direct: 8-15% gas savings = $200K-1M/year savings for a typical tile plant running 24/7.

21	## Step 1: Technology / Science Advancement Research
22	
23	**Objective**: Identify 10 recent technologies or scientific findings that are ready (or within 6–12 months of ready) for real-world product implementation.
24	
25	### Search Strategy
26	- Academic preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv, Nature, Science) for papers with "practical", "real-time", "low-cost", "scalable" in abstracts from the last 12 months
27	- Patent filings (Google Patents, USPTO) showing implementation-ready claims
28	- Tech press (TechCrunch, Ars Technica, IEEE Spectrum, MIT Tech Review) for "breakthrough" announcements
29	- Conference proceedings (NeurIPS, ICML, CES, IEDM, ACM) from last 2 cycles
30	- Government grants/SBIR awards signaling commercialization readiness
31	- GitHub trending repos with rapid star growth in novel domains
32	
33	### Domains to Scan (rotate across cycles)
34	- Materials science & manufacturing (metamaterials, bio-fabrication, novel batteries)
35	- Biotech & health (diagnostics, therapeutics, wearables, synthetic biology)
36	- AI/ML applied to physical systems (robotics, autonomous systems, edge AI)
37	- Energy & sustainability (carbon capture, grid storage, fusion-adjacent)
38	- Quantum computing applications (not the hardware — the use cases becoming practical)
39	- Space tech (smallsat, in-space manufacturing, Earth observation)
40	- Human-computer interaction (BCI, spatial computing, haptics)
41	- Food & agriculture tech (precision ag, alternative proteins, vertical farming)

43	### Promotion Criteria (must meet ALL)
44	| Criterion | Threshold |
45	|-----------|-----------|
46	| Technology Readiness Level (TRL) | ≥ 5 (validated in relevant environment) |
47	| Time to first product | ≤ 18 months from today |
48	| Key enabling breakthrough | Clearly identified (cost reduction, miniaturization, accuracy jump, etc.) |
49	| Reproducibility | Demonstrated by ≥ 2 independent groups OR open-sourced |
50	| Not purely incremental | Represents a step-change, not a marginal improvement |

52	### Rejection Reasons (any one disqualifies)
53	- Still lab-only with no path to scale (TRL < 4)
54	- Requires regulatory approval > 3 years out (e.g., novel drug, nuclear)
55	- Fundamental physics/engineering barriers unresolved
56	- Already well-known and widely covered (e.g., LLMs themselves — too late)

99	## Step 3: Market Analysis
100	
101	**Objective**: For technologies promoted from Step 2, identify target markets and potential products, then size the opportunity.
102	
103	### Process
104	1. **Product ideation**: For each technology, brainstorm 3–5 specific products/solutions it enables
105	2. **Market identification**: For each product, identify the target customer segment and industry vertical
106	3. **Market sizing** (TAM/SAM/SOM):
107	   - **TAM** (Total Addressable Market): Total revenue opportunity if 100% market share
108	   - **SAM** (Serviceable Addressable Market): Segment you can realistically reach
109	   - **SOM** (Serviceable Obtainable Market): What you could capture in 3–5 years
110	4. **Revenue model**: How would the product make money? (SaaS, hardware, marketplace, licensing, etc.)
111	
112	### Market Sizing Methods
113	- **Top-down**: Industry reports (Statista, Grand View Research, IBISWorld) → narrow to segment
114	- **Bottom-up**: Number of potential customers × willingness to pay × purchase frequency
115	- **Analogous**: Compare to similar products in adjacent markets
116	
117	### Promotion Criteria
118	| Criterion | Threshold |
119	|-----------|-----------|
120	| TAM | > $1B |
121	| SAM | > $100M |
122	| Growth rate | > 15% CAGR |
123	| Clear buyer persona | Identifiable decision-maker with budget |
124	| Willingness to pay | Evidence of spending in adjacent solutions |
125	
126	### Rejection Reasons
127	- Market too small/niche (SAM < $50M)
128	- Declining market
129	- No clear buyer (technology looking for a problem)
130	- Regulatory barriers to market entry in most geographies

161	
162	| Tailwinds (accelerators) | Headwinds (blockers) |

165	| Declining component costs | Supply chain risks |
166	| Cultural/behavioral shifts | Customer inertia / switching costs |
167	| Platform shifts enabling distribution | Incumbent lock-in |
168	| Adjacent ecosystem maturity | Missing infrastructure |
169	| Talent availability improving | Scarce specialized talent |

**Idea slug:** `wirevision_ai`
**Type:** HW + SW (commodity cameras + edge AI + dashboard)
**Date:** 2026-06-28
**Researcher:** Step-6 deep-research pass
**One-line pitch:** Inline AI surface-defect inspection for wire/cable extrusion lines on commodity cameras at ~15% of the cost of SIKORA / Pixargus systems, targeting the mid-market that can't justify $80–150K legacy rigs.

**Verdict: CONDITIONAL GO (lean toward NO-GO as a SECOND business for this founder).** The market gap is real and the tech is feasible, but this is a **hardware-bearing, field-installed, conservative-buyer industrial play** that conflicts with the founder's "pure-software secondary income stream" goal. It is a credible venture-scale company for a full-time team — but a poor #2 nights-and-weekends bet versus a pure-SaaS idea. See Scorecard (Section 5).

---

## 1. Product Definition

### Exact problem statement
Wire and cable extrusion lines (building wire, automotive harness wire, power cord, telecom/data cable, hose, tube) produce continuous product at 200–1500 m/min. Surface defects — **lumps, neckdowns, scrapes, gels, insulation pinholes, discoloration, diameter excursions, eccentricity** — cause customer returns, warranty claims, and scrap. Today the buyer has three options:

1. **Spark tester only** ($5–15K): finds pinholes/insulation faults via high voltage, but is **blind to surface/dimensional defects**. (VERIFIED — Clinton Instrument / standard industry tooling.)
2. **Full optical surface inspection** ($80–200K): SIKORA, Pixargus ProfilControl, LaserLinc FlawSense, Zumbach. Multi-camera laser-calibrated rigs. (VERIFIED — see Section 2.)
3. **Manual/visual + offline lab QC**: operators eyeball the line and pull samples. Misses most defects; reactive not preventive. (ASSUMED — standard mid-market practice.)

The pain: a mid-market manufacturer ($5–50M revenue, 5–50 lines) lives in the gap between option 1 and option 2. They have real quality problems (especially as EV, solar, datacenter, and aerospace customers tighten specs) but cannot justify $100K+/line.

### Product scope for v1 (3 features max)
1. **Real-time surface-defect detection & classification** (lump, neckdown, scrape, discoloration, gel) on commodity cameras with edge inference, with a per-meter defect map.
2. **Diameter / lump dimensional flagging** (single-axis, camera-based — NOT a metrology-grade replacement for laser micrometers).
3. **Dashboard + SPC**: defect log, location tagging (encoder-synced), trend charts, exportable QC report per spool/run.

### Explicitly does NOT do (v1)
